q: A 22-year-old has palpitations. His resting ECG is shown. The characteristic finding is
e: Short PR with slurred QRS upstroke = delta wave of Wolff–Parkinson–White (accessory pathway). In pre-excited AF avoid AV-nodal blockers (adenosine, verapamil, digoxin, beta-blockers); give procainamide or cardiovert if unstable.

q: This ECG shows tall, narrow-based peaked T waves. The most likely abnormality and the first drug are
e: Peaked T waves are the earliest ECG sign of hyperkalaemia. Membrane stabilisation with IV calcium gluconate comes first, then insulin–dextrose, salbutamol, bicarbonate if acidotic, and removal (loop diuretic, resin, dialysis).

q: A 58-year-old man has chest pain. ECG shows convex ST elevation across V1–V4. The culprit artery is
e: ST elevation in V1–V4 is an anterior STEMI: LAD territory. Primary PCI within 90 minutes of first medical contact; fibrinolysis if PCI cannot be done within 120 minutes.

q: A patient has sudden right hemiparesis. The NCCT head sign shown indicates
o: Thrombus in the middle cerebral artery
e: A hyperdense MCA sign is an early CT sign of acute thrombus in the MCA. Treat with IV alteplase/tenecteplase within 4.5 h if eligible, and consider mechanical thrombectomy for large-vessel occlusion.

q: Which imaging modality is most sensitive for detecting hyperacute ischaemic stroke within minutes of onset?
e: DWI shows restricted diffusion (bright signal) within minutes. NCCT is still the first test because it excludes haemorrhage quickly.

q: A 17-year-old has tremor and abnormal LFTs. A slit-lamp image of the eye is shown. The best initial confirmatory test is
e: Kayser–Fleischer ring points to Wilson disease: low serum ceruloplasmin, raised 24-hour urinary copper, hepatic copper >250 µg/g dry weight. Treatment is chelation (D-penicillamine, trientine) and zinc.

q: A silver stain of a glomerulus shows 'spikes' along a thickened basement membrane. The most specific serum antibody in primary disease is
e: Spike-and-dome pattern with subepithelial deposits is membranous nephropathy; most primary cases have anti-PLA2R antibody. IF shows granular IgG and C3.

q: Crescentic glomerulonephritis with linear IgG on immunofluorescence is caused by antibodies against
o: α3 chain of type IV collagen (NC1 domain)
e: Anti-GBM disease (Goodpasture): antibody to the α3(IV) collagen NC1 domain; treat with plasma exchange, steroids and cyclophosphamide.

q: This glomerulus shows PAS-positive acellular nodules in the mesangium. The most likely cause is
e: Kimmelstiel–Wilson nodular glomerulosclerosis is classic for diabetic nephropathy. Amyloid would stain with Congo red and show apple-green birefringence.

q: A farmer bitten in the field develops bleeding gums, haematuria and oliguria. The snake in the image is most likely
e: A chain of dark oval blotches along the back and triangular head is Russell's viper: haemotoxic (VICC, AKI). Give polyvalent ASV; use the 20-minute whole blood clotting test to monitor.

q: The patient shown has proptosis with lid retraction. The antibody responsible is directed against
e: Graves disease: TSH-receptor-stimulating antibody (TRAb). Anti-TPO is positive in Hashimoto and also commonly in Graves, but TRAb is the pathogenic and most specific antibody.

q: This ¹²³I-MIBG scan shows focal uptake in the left adrenal region. Before surgery the first drug to start is
e: Pheochromocytoma: start an alpha blocker (phenoxybenzamine or doxazosin) first, then a beta blocker. Beta blockade alone can precipitate a hypertensive crisis through unopposed alpha stimulation.

q: A peripheral smear from a febrile traveller shows multiple ring forms and banana-shaped gametocytes. The species is
e: Multiple rings per cell, appliqué forms and crescent gametocytes are diagnostic of P. falciparum. Severe malaria is treated with IV artesunate.

q: A patient recovering from fever develops a confluent erythematous rash with islands of spared white skin. The diagnosis is
e: 'Islands of white in a sea of red' is the convalescent rash of dengue. Watch for the critical phase at defervescence (plasma leakage, fall in platelets, rising haematocrit).

q: Urine sediment shows muddy-brown granular casts. The diagnosis is
e: Muddy-brown granular and epithelial cell casts = ATN. WBC casts suggest pyelonephritis/interstitial nephritis; RBC casts suggest glomerulonephritis.

q: The chest X-ray shows bilateral diffuse opacities without cardiomegaly after sepsis. The ventilator strategy proven to reduce mortality is
o: Low tidal volume 6 ml/kg of predicted body weight
e: ARDS (Berlin: acute onset, bilateral opacities, PaO2/FiO2 ≤300 on PEEP ≥5). Use lung-protective ventilation (6 ml/kg PBW, plateau pressure <30), and prone positioning for severe ARDS.

q: The smear shows microcytic hypochromic cells with pencil cells. The test that best confirms the diagnosis is
e: Iron deficiency: low serum ferritin is the most specific test; high TIBC, low transferrin saturation. Ferritin is an acute phase reactant, so a value up to about 100 µg/L can still be deficient in inflammation.

q: Fragmented red cells (schistocytes) are NOT a feature of
e: Schistocytes mean microangiopathic haemolysis (HUS, TTP, DIC, malignant hypertension, mechanical valves). Hereditary spherocytosis shows spherocytes.

q: The facial appearance shown is due to excess GH. The best confirmatory test is
o: Failure of GH suppression on an oral glucose tolerance test
e: Screen with IGF-1; confirm with the OGTT (GH fails to fall below ~1 ng/ml). Then MRI pituitary; first-line treatment is transsphenoidal surgery.

q: A young man with syncope has coved ST elevation and an inverted T wave in V1. The best management is
e: Brugada type 1 pattern (SCN5A in about a quarter): ICD for symptomatic patients; avoid sodium-channel blockers, treat fever. Quinidine is an adjunct.

q: A patient with CD4 50/µl has dry cough and exertional dyspnoea. The chest X-ray shows bilateral perihilar ground-glass opacities. The treatment is
e: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia: high-dose co-trimoxazole for 21 days, plus prednisolone if hypoxaemic. Prophylaxis when CD4 <200.

q: A patient with ulcerative colitis has fever and tachycardia; the abdominal X-ray shows a transverse colon of 7 cm. Which should be avoided?
e: Toxic megacolon (colon >6 cm with toxicity): IV steroids, fluids, antibiotics, early surgical review; avoid colonoscopy/barium (perforation) and antimotility drugs.

q: This CT shows blood in the basal cisterns. The drug given to prevent delayed cerebral ischaemia is
e: Nimodipine (calcium channel blocker) 60 mg 4-hourly for 21 days improves outcome after aneurysmal SAH. Secure the aneurysm early (clipping or coiling).

q: HRCT shows subpleural reticulation with honeycombing and traction bronchiectasis. The best treatment option to slow progression is
e: UIP pattern = IPF. Antifibrotics (pirfenidone, nintedanib) slow FVC decline; steroids are not useful and harmful in IPF. Lung transplant is definitive.

q: A patient with hypotension has the CT finding shown. The best treatment is
e: Saddle embolus with haemodynamic instability = high-risk PE: systemic thrombolysis (alteplase) unless contraindicated; surgical or catheter embolectomy otherwise.

q: Synovial fluid under compensated polarised light shows needle-shaped crystals that are yellow when parallel to the axis. They are
e: Monosodium urate crystals are needle-shaped and strongly negatively birefringent (yellow parallel). CPPD crystals are rhomboid and weakly positively birefringent.

q: A trauma patient is hypotensive with absent breath sounds on the left, tracheal shift and distended neck veins. The immediate step is
o: Needle decompression at the 4th/5th intercostal space, just anterior to the mid-axillary line
e: Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis. ATLS 10th edition places decompression at the 4th–5th ICS anterior to the mid-axillary line, followed by a chest drain.

q: By the rule of nines in an adult, the burn surface area of one entire lower limb is
e: Adult rule of nines: head and neck 9, each upper limb 9, anterior trunk 18, posterior trunk 18, each lower limb 18, perineum 1. In children the head is larger and legs smaller (Lund–Browder).

q: A biconvex hyperdense lesion limited by sutures is seen after a temporal bone fracture. The vessel involved is
e: Extradural haematoma: middle meningeal artery, lucid interval, lentiform on CT; urgent evacuation. Subdural haematoma arises from bridging veins and is crescentic.

q: An elderly man on warfarin falls. CT shows a crescentic collection over the convexity crossing sutures with midline shift. The source is
e: Subdural haematoma: tearing of bridging veins; common in elderly and anticoagulated patients; crosses sutures but not dural reflections.

q: A thyroid nodule FNAC shows nuclei with optical clearing and grooves. The commonest route of spread is
e: Papillary carcinoma: Orphan Annie eye nuclei, psammoma bodies; spreads via lymphatics; excellent prognosis. Follicular carcinoma spreads haematogenously.

q: A preterm neonate on feeds develops abdominal distension and bloody stools. The X-ray finding shown is
e: Necrotising enterocolitis: pneumatosis intestinalis, portal venous gas; surgery for perforation (free air), clinical deterioration or fixed loop. Bell staging guides care.

q: This abdominal film of an elderly constipated man shows a huge inverted-U loop. The first step in a stable patient without peritonitis is
o: Sigmoidoscopic decompression with a flatus tube
e: Sigmoid volvulus (coffee-bean sign): endoscopic detorsion first; elective sigmoid colectomy later because recurrence is high. Peritonitis or ischaemia needs surgery.

q: A 9-month-old has colicky pain, red-currant jelly stool and this ultrasound finding. Treatment of choice in a stable child is
e: Intussusception: target (doughnut) sign on USG; image-guided enema reduction unless peritonitis or perforation. Pathologic lead points are more likely in older children.

q: A patient with sudden epigastric pain has this erect chest film. The commonest cause is
e: Free gas under the diaphragm means a perforated hollow viscus; the commonest cause is a perforated duodenal ulcer. Treat with resuscitation, antibiotics and surgery (omental patch).

q: A barium swallow shows a dilated oesophagus with a tapered 'bird's beak' lower end. The gold-standard diagnostic test is
e: Achalasia: manometry shows incomplete LES relaxation with aperistalsis. Treat with Heller myotomy, POEM or pneumatic dilatation; endoscopy first excludes pseudoachalasia (cancer).

q: A woman has painless vaginal bleeding at membrane rupture followed by fetal bradycardia. The finding on Doppler is
e: Vasa previa: unsupported fetal vessels over the internal os; fetal exsanguination at rupture. Elective caesarean at 34–36 weeks; steroids for lung maturity.

q: The image shows placental villi invading through the uterine wall to the serosa. The strongest risk factor is
e: Placenta accreta spectrum (accreta → increta → percreta). Risk rises with number of prior caesareans plus previa. Plan caesarean hysterectomy with the placenta left in situ.

q: Bilateral ovarian masses show signet-ring cells in a desmoplastic stroma. The primary is most often in the
e: Krukenberg tumours: metastases with mucin-secreting signet-ring cells, most often from the stomach (also colon, breast). Usually bilateral.

q: A 25-year-old has a cystic ovarian mass containing hair and sebaceous material. The commonest complication is
e: Mature cystic teratoma (dermoid) is the commonest ovarian germ cell tumour; torsion is the commonest complication. Malignant change (squamous carcinoma) is rare and mostly in postmenopausal women.

q: A pregnant woman with a known fibroid has severe localised pain and low-grade fever. The gross picture of the specimen suggests
e: Red degeneration is haemorrhagic infarction of a fibroid in pregnancy; manage conservatively with analgesia and rest. Surgery is rarely needed.

q: A child with fever, cough and conjunctivitis has these oral spots. The essential adjunct treatment is
e: Koplik spots = measles. All children with measles get vitamin A (200,000 IU if ≥12 months) for 2 days. Complications: pneumonia, SSPE.

q: A child with 'slapped cheek' erythema is infected with an organism that causes aplastic crisis in
e: Erythema infectiosum: parvovirus B19. It infects erythroid precursors → transient aplastic crisis in chronic haemolysis (e.g. sickle cell, spherocytosis) and hydrops fetalis in pregnancy.

q: A toddler has oval vesicles on palms and soles with oral ulcers. The commonest agent is
e: Hand–foot–mouth disease: Coxsackie A16, enterovirus 71 (neurological complications). Supportive care.

q: This X-ray shows a boot-shaped heart with oligaemic lung fields in a cyanotic child. The immediate management of a hypercyanotic spell is
e: Tetralogy of Fallot: knee–chest position, oxygen, morphine, IV fluids, phenylephrine/propranolol, bicarbonate; definitive surgery (BT shunt or complete repair).

q: A cyanotic newborn has an 'egg on a string' cardiac silhouette with increased pulmonary vascularity. The first drug is
e: Transposition of the great arteries: PGE1 to keep the ductus open, balloon atrial septostomy, then arterial switch within the first 1–2 weeks.

q: A 29-week preterm has grunting shortly after birth; the X-ray shows ground-glass opacities with air bronchograms. The treatment is
e: Respiratory distress syndrome (surfactant deficiency): CPAP and early surfactant, antenatal steroids prevent it. Lecithin:sphingomyelin ratio <2 indicates immaturity.

q: A child has pedal oedema, flag sign and angular stomatitis. According to WHO the diagnosis is
e: Bilateral pitting oedema = severe acute malnutrition (kwashiorkor), regardless of weight-for-height. Stabilise with F-75, then F-100 or RUTF, and treat hypoglycaemia, hypothermia and infection.

q: An infant has widened wrists and rachitic rosary. The earliest biochemical abnormality in nutritional rickets is
o: Raised alkaline phosphatase with low 25-OH vitamin D
e: Nutritional rickets: low 25-OH vitamin D, raised ALP and PTH, low/normal calcium and low phosphate. X-ray: cupping, fraying, splaying. Treat with vitamin D 'stoss' therapy plus calcium.

q: A child with night blindness has foamy triangular conjunctival patches. The therapeutic dose of vitamin A for a child over 1 year is
e: Bitot spots (X1B). WHO treatment: 200,000 IU orally on day 1, day 2 and 2 weeks later (half dose for infants 6–12 months, quarter for under 6 months).

q: The optic disc shown has a large vertical cup with nasal displacement of vessels. Which feature favours glaucoma over physiological cupping?
o: Thinning of the neuroretinal rim violating the ISNT rule
e: Glaucomatous disc: vertical elongation, rim thinning (ISNT rule broken), bayoneting, notching, nasal vessel displacement, asymmetry >0.2.

q: An infant has photophobia, tearing and an enlarged cornea. The definitive treatment is
e: Primary congenital glaucoma (buphthalmos, Haab striae): surgery (goniotomy/trabeculotomy) is the treatment of choice; medical therapy is only a bridge.

q: A young obese woman has headache and bilateral disc swelling with normal vision and pupils. The next step is
o: Neuroimaging, then lumbar puncture with opening pressure
e: Papilloedema indicates raised intracranial pressure. Image first (exclude mass), then LP; idiopathic intracranial hypertension is treated with acetazolamide and weight loss.

q: New vessels on the disc/retina define
e: Proliferative DR (NVD/NVE) is treated with panretinal photocoagulation and/or anti-VEGF; vitrectomy for vitreous haemorrhage or traction.

q: A patient has sudden painless loss of vision with a cherry-red spot at the macula. The diagnosis is
e: CRAO: pale oedematous retina with a cherry-red spot and narrowed arterioles; an ocular emergency. Look for embolic source (carotid, heart) and giant cell arteritis.

q: A child presents with a white pupillary reflex. The gene involved in the most likely tumour is
e: Leukocoria is the commonest presentation of retinoblastoma (RB1, 13q14, tumour suppressor). Calcification on imaging; avoid biopsy.

q: A branching corneal ulcer with terminal end-bulbs is stained with fluorescein. Which treatment is contraindicated?
e: HSV dendritic keratitis: topical or oral antivirals; steroids worsen epithelial disease. Steroids are reserved for stromal keratitis under antiviral cover.

q: Layered pus in the inferior anterior chamber seen with a painful red eye is called
e: Hypopyon: sterile in HLA-B27 uveitis and Behçet disease; infective in bacterial or fungal keratitis (fungal keratitis hypopyon is non-mobile).

q: A child with chronic discharge has granulation tissue at the pars flaccida. The treatment is
o: Mastoid exploration (canal wall up or down mastoidectomy)
e: Attic granulation signals attico-antral (unsafe) CSOM with cholesteatoma; surgical clearance via mastoidectomy is needed to prevent complications.

q: An infant has inspiratory stridor worse when supine and feeding. Laryngoscopy shows an omega-shaped epiglottis. The management is
e: Laryngomalacia is the commonest cause of congenital stridor and usually self-resolves; surgery (supraglottoplasty) only for severe cases with failure to thrive or apnoea.

q: A patient with a tooth infection has woody, brawny bilateral submandibular swelling and trismus. The first priority is
e: Ludwig's angina: bilateral submandibular space cellulitis, airway compromise. Secure the airway, IV antibiotics, drainage if collection.

q: A 15-year-old has knee pain and this sclerotic metaphyseal lesion. The mainstay of treatment is
o: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy, limb-salvage surgery, adjuvant chemotherapy
e: Osteosarcoma: commonest site distal femur metaphysis; ALP raised; Codman triangle and sunburst. Chest CT for metastases.

q: A teenager has night pain relieved by aspirin and this CT. Preferred treatment is
e: Osteoid osteoma: nidus <1.5 cm with surrounding sclerosis, night pain relieved by NSAIDs (PGE2); CT-guided radiofrequency ablation is first line.

q: The hand deformity shown (claw of the ring and little fingers) indicates injury to
e: Ulnar claw hand with Froment's sign positive; lesion at the wrist produces a more marked claw than a high lesion (ulnar paradox).

q: An 8-year-old falls on an outstretched hand; the elbow X-ray shows the fracture. The nerve most commonly injured is
e: Extension-type supracondylar fracture: anterior interosseous nerve (median branch) is commonly injured; brachial artery compromise causes Volkmann ischaemic contracture.

q: A fracture of the distal radius with dorsal displacement is classically described as
e: Colles fracture: dinner-fork deformity, dorsal angulation, fall on outstretched hand in older women. Smith's is the reverse (volar displacement, 'garden spade').

q: An obese 12-year-old has hip pain and limp; the frog-leg view shows the epiphysis slipped off the neck. The treatment is
o: In situ pinning with a single screw
e: SCFE: do not reduce forcibly (avascular necrosis); in situ pinning; non-weight-bearing immediately. Klein's line fails to intersect the epiphysis.

q: Direct immunofluorescence shows intercellular IgG in a fishnet pattern. The target antigen is
e: Pemphigus vulgaris: anti-Dsg3 (± Dsg1), suprabasal acantholysis, positive Nikolsky sign, flaccid bullae. Treat with steroids and rituximab.

q: An elderly woman has tense bullae. The target antigen is
e: Bullous pemphigoid: subepidermal blister, linear IgG/C3 at the basement membrane zone; targets BP180 and BP230 in hemidesmosomes.

q: A hypopigmented patch on the thigh is evaluated. The first bedside test is
e: Leprosy: loss of sensation in a skin patch, thickened nerve, or acid-fast bacilli on slit-skin smear. WHO operational classification: PB ≤5 lesions, MB >5.

q: A thin wavy burrow between the finger web spaces with nocturnal itching is treated with
e: Scabies (Sarcoptes scabiei): permethrin 5% from neck down, repeated after 7 days; treat contacts; ivermectin oral for crusted or outbreaks.

q: Silvery-scaled plaques on extensor surfaces; scale removal shows pinpoint bleeding. This is called
e: Auspitz sign (pinpoint bleeding on removing scale) is typical of psoriasis. Koebner is new lesions at sites of trauma (also in lichen planus, vitiligo).

q: Flat-topped violaceous itchy papules with lacy white lines. The lines are called
e: Lichen planus: purple, polygonal, pruritic, planar, papules; Wickham striae; oral lesions; Koebner phenomenon; saw-tooth infiltrate on histology.

q: A larger oval scaly patch followed a week later by smaller oval lesions along skin lines. Diagnosis:
e: Pityriasis rosea: herald patch then 'Christmas tree' distribution along cleavage lines; self-limiting. Check VDRL if the palms and soles are involved.

q: The most important prognostic factor in cutaneous melanoma is
e: Breslow thickness (depth in mm) determines prognosis and excision margins; ABCDE rule for recognition; sentinel node biopsy for T1b and above (>0.8 mm or ulcerated).

q: A newborn with vomiting has the X-ray shown. The commonest associated syndrome is
e: Double bubble with no distal gas = duodenal atresia, associated with Down syndrome (about a third). Bilious vomiting in the first day.

q: A supine AP film of a trauma patient shows a deep lucent costophrenic sulcus. This suggests
e: Deep sulcus sign on a supine film indicates anterior pneumothorax; ultrasound (absent lung sliding) and CT are more sensitive.

q: A smear shows a promyelocyte packed with Auer rods in a patient with DIC. The translocation and treatment are
e: APL: t(15;17) PML–RARA; ATRA ± arsenic trioxide; DIC is the major early threat, so start ATRA immediately on suspicion.

q: B cells with hair-like projections, dry tap and splenomegaly. The marker/mutation is
e: Hairy cell leukaemia: TRAP positive, CD11c/CD25/CD103, annexin A1, BRAF V600E; treated with cladribine.

q: Tumour cells palisading around necrosis in an adult brain tumour. The diagnosis is
e: Glioblastoma (IDH-wildtype): pseudopalisading necrosis and microvascular proliferation; butterfly glioma crossing the corpus callosum.

q: Eosinophilic corkscrew Rosenthal fibres are seen in
e: Pilocytic astrocytoma: children, cerebellum, cyst with mural nodule, BRAF fusion, Rosenthal fibres and eosinophilic granular bodies; best prognosis.

q: A child's midline cerebellar tumour shows small blue cells forming Homer Wright rosettes. This tumour is
e: Medulloblastoma: Homer Wright rosettes; synaptophysin positive; CSF drop metastases; SHH, WNT subtypes. Ependymoma shows perivascular pseudorosettes.

q: The smear shows small dense red cells without central pallor. The best confirmatory test is
e: Hereditary spherocytosis: ankyrin/spectrin defects; EMA binding (flow cytometry) is the most sensitive; osmotic fragility test; DAT is negative; splenectomy for severe cases.

q: The molecular defect in sickle cell anaemia is
o: Glutamic acid to valine at position 6 of the β-globin chain
Glutamic acid to lysine at position 6
e: HbS: Glu6Val (GAG→GTG) in β-globin. HbC is Glu6Lys. Hydroxyurea raises HbF.

q: A large binucleate cell with 'owl-eye' nucleoli is seen in a lymph node biopsy. The immunophenotype is
e: Reed–Sternberg cell: classical Hodgkin lymphoma is CD15+, CD30+, CD45−; nodular lymphocyte predominant is CD20+ CD15−.

q: 'Starry sky' appearance with tingible-body macrophages is characteristic of a lymphoma with
e: Burkitt lymphoma: t(8;14) MYC–IGH; EBV in endemic form; very high proliferation (Ki-67 ~100%); tumour lysis syndrome risk.

q: Concentrically laminated basophilic calcifications are NOT typical of
e: Psammoma bodies: papillary thyroid carcinoma, serous ovarian carcinoma, meningioma, mesothelioma, prolactinoma/somatostatinoma (PSAMMOMA). Follicular thyroid carcinoma lacks them.

q: Congo red staining viewed under crossed polarisers shows apple-green birefringence. This is due to
e: Amyloid is a β-pleated sheet fibrillar protein; Congo red apple-green birefringence is diagnostic. AL (light chains), AA (SAA), ATTR (transthyretin) are common types.

q: A lymph node shows central caseation surrounded by epithelioid cells and Langhans giant cells. The giant cell nuclei are arranged
o: In a wreath around the nucleoli only
e: Langhans giant cells (TB) have nuclei in a horseshoe at the periphery; foreign body giant cells have random nuclei. Granuloma requires CD4 T cells and IFN-γ.

q: Teardrop cells with leucoerythroblastic picture and dry tap. The most frequent driver mutation is
e: Primary myelofibrosis: JAK2 V617F ~50–60%, CALR ~25%, MPL; treatment ruxolitinib. Teardrop cells are due to extramedullary haematopoiesis and fibrosis.

q: Albert stain shows green bacilli with bluish-black granules in Chinese-letter arrangement. The organism is
e: Metachromatic (Babes–Ernst/Volutin) granules in C. diphtheriae; culture on Loeffler's serum slope and tellurite blood agar; toxin tested by Elek test.

q: This Ziehl–Neelsen smear of sputum shows slender pink-red bacilli on a blue background. Acid-fastness is due to
o: Mycolic acid in the cell wall
e: Mycobacteria retain carbol fuchsin after acid–alcohol decolourisation because of long-chain mycolic acids. M. leprae is weakly acid-fast (decolourised with 5% H2SO4); Nocardia is partially acid-fast.

q: A diabetic in ketoacidosis has facial pain and black nasal discharge; the biopsy shows broad ribbon-like hyphae. The drug is
e: Mucormycosis: non-septate hyphae with right-angle branching; surgical debridement + amphotericin B; control hyperglycaemia and acidosis; isavuconazole/posaconazole as step-down.

q: An HIV patient has meningitis; the India ink preparation is shown. The best rapid test is
e: Cryptococcus neoformans: encapsulated yeast; CrAg in CSF/serum is most sensitive; induction with amphotericin B + flucytosine, repeated LP for raised pressure.

q: Eosinophilic intracytoplasmic neuronal inclusions are seen in rabies. They are called
e: Negri bodies (hippocampus, Purkinje cells); diagnosis by direct fluorescent antibody on nuchal skin biopsy. Cowdry A is herpes; Guarnieri is variola.

q: Gram-positive cocci in grape-like clusters, catalase positive and coagulase positive. The organism is
e: Staph aureus: catalase +, coagulase +, mannitol fermenter; MRSA via mecA (PBP2a). S. saprophyticus is novobiocin resistant and causes UTI in young women.

q: Gram-positive cocci in chains, catalase negative, beta-haemolytic, bacitracin sensitive. The organism is
e: Group A streptococcus: bacitracin sensitive, PYR positive; S. agalactiae (GBS) is bacitracin resistant, CAMP and hippurate positive.

q: Dependent purple discolouration with pale pressure areas is seen. It becomes fixed in about
e: Postmortem lividity appears in 1–2 h, merges by 4–6 h, fixed by about 6–8 h. Before fixation it shifts if the body is moved. Cherry-red lividity: CO and cyanide poisoning.

q: Basophilic stippling in red cells with a blue line on the gums points to poisoning with
e: Lead poisoning: basophilic stippling (pyrimidine 5'-nucleotidase and ALA dehydratase inhibition), Burton's line, wrist drop, microcytic anaemia; chelate with CaNa2EDTA or succimer.

q: An epidemic curve with a sharp rise and fall within one incubation period, with an index case, suggests
e: Common-source (single exposure) outbreak: explosive rise and fall within one incubation period. A propagated outbreak shows successive peaks one incubation period apart.

q: An epidemic curve with successive peaks separated by about one incubation period is typical of
e: Propagated (person-to-person) epidemics show serial waves; measles and polio are examples.

q: In the cavernous sinus, which cranial nerve lies free within the sinus lumen alongside the ICA?
e: III, IV, V1, V2 lie in the lateral wall; VI (abducens) lies inside the sinus with the ICA and sympathetic plexus, so it is affected first in cavernous sinus thrombosis.

q: In the Circle of Willis, the vessel joining the two anterior cerebral arteries is the
e: Anterior communicating connects the two ACAs; posterior communicating connects ICA with PCA. The MCA is not part of the circle. Commonest berry aneurysm site: ACom/ACA junction.

q: Bluish-grey pigmentation of the ear cartilage with dark urine on standing. The deficient enzyme is
e: Alkaptonuria (ochronosis): homogentisate 1,2-dioxygenase deficiency; arthritis, dark urine; treat with nitisinone.

q: Macrophages with 'crumpled tissue paper' cytoplasm are seen in bone marrow. The deficient enzyme is
e: Gaucher disease (commonest LSD): glucocerebrosidase deficiency; hepatosplenomegaly, bone crises; enzyme replacement imiglucerase.

q: A peripheral smear shows a myeloblast containing the needle-like cytoplasmic inclusion shown. This inclusion is composed of
e: Auer rods = fused lysosomal (primary) granules, myeloperoxidase positive; pathognomonic of myeloid lineage (AML), numerous "faggot cells" in APL t(15;17) — start ATRA at suspicion.

q: Congo red-stained tissue viewed under crossed polarisers shows the finding illustrated. The underlying protein conformation is
e: Apple-green birefringence on Congo red = amyloid, whose fibrils are β-pleated sheets irrespective of precursor protein (AL, AA, ATTR, Aβ2M).

q: A person dies of encephalitis after a dog bite. Brain histology shows the inclusion in a cerebellar Purkinje cell. The inclusion is
e: Negri bodies: eosinophilic cytoplasmic inclusions of rabies (hippocampal pyramidal cells and cerebellar Purkinje cells). Absence does not exclude rabies; FAT on skin biopsy / brain is preferred.

q: BAL from an HIV-positive patient (CD4 80/µL) with dry cough and hypoxia shows these cysts on silver stain. The drug of choice is
e: Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia: cotrimoxazole 21 days; add prednisolone if PaO₂ <70 mmHg. Prophylaxis when CD4 <200.

q: Slit-lamp examination of a child with multiple café-au-lait macules shows these iris lesions. They are
e: Lisch nodules = NF1 iris hamartomas (>90% of adults). Koeppe/Busacca are inflammatory (granulomatous uveitis); Brushfield spots occur in Down syndrome.

q: A 2-year-old has barking cough, stridor and low-grade fever. The neck radiograph sign illustrated is
e: Steeple (pencil-point) sign on AP view in croup, parainfluenza virus; treat with dexamethasone, nebulised adrenaline if stridor at rest. Thumb sign (lateral) = epiglottitis.

q: A toxic-looking, drooling child in tripod position with high fever. The lateral neck film shows the finding illustrated. The first priority is
o: Secure the airway by an experienced anaesthetist/ENT in OR
Examine the throat with a tongue depressor
Start oral antibiotics and send home
e: Thumb sign = swollen epiglottis (acute epiglottitis, H. influenzae b, now rare after Hib vaccine). Do NOT upset the child or examine the throat; secure the airway first, then ceftriaxone.

q: An elderly man has increasing hat size, deafness and bone pain. Serum ALP is markedly raised with normal calcium and phosphate. The skull shows this thickening. The most dreaded complication is
e: Paget disease of bone: ↑osteoclast activity then disorganised sclerosis, mosaic pattern; cotton-wool skull. High-output cardiac failure and osteosarcoma (1%) are complications. Treat with bisphosphonates.

q: A young patient has these three-zone lesions on the legs 1 week after herpes labialis. The diagnosis is
e: Typical target lesions (dusky centre, pale ring, erythematous halo) = erythema multiforme minor, usually HSV-triggered; SJS/TEN is drug-induced with <10% / >30% BSA detachment and mucosal erosions.

q: A 14-year-old obese girl has velvety dark pigmentation of the axillae. The best next test is
e: Acanthosis nigricans in an obese teen = insulin resistance (type 2 DM, PCOS). Sudden-onset extensive disease in an older adult suggests visceral malignancy (gastric adenocarcinoma).

q: A woman has proximal muscle weakness and these violaceous papules over the knuckles. The associated autoantibody that most strongly predicts malignancy is
e: Gottron papules = dermatomyositis. Anti-TIF1γ and anti-NXP2 are linked to cancer; anti-Jo-1 to anti-synthetase syndrome (ILD, mechanic hands); anti-Mi-2 to classic skin disease with good prognosis.

q: A young adult has painless cervical lymphadenopathy and night sweats. The binucleate cell with prominent nucleoli on biopsy is positive for
e: Reed-Sternberg cell: CD15+ CD30+, CD45−, CD20 usually −. Nodular lymphocyte-predominant HL has LP cells that are CD20+ and CD15−. Mixed-cellularity / EBV association.
